New York Bight · Hurricane Sandy flood hindcast · SFINCS with the SnapWave wave model

Sandy Hindcast, Plainly

What the model is, how well it works, what we learned between 2 and 10 September 2026, and what is running now. Written for the 10 September meeting, for a reader who has not followed the week, and updated on the morning of the 10th with the first two results.

State of play

The model is good on the open ocean and low almost everywhere behind it

The model reproduces Sandy’s storm tide at the open-ocean gauge to within a centimetre and floods the right places: 87 % of the 94 surveyed high-water marks we score are matched to within half a metre. But it runs low. The marks average 16 cm below what was surveyed, the gauges inside the southern bays sit 20 to 55 cm below the observations, and that gap is already there on the quiet day before the storm. This week we traced it to the wave model: the waves we feed in at the seaward edge of the model are not reaching the beach. The first fix, a geometric one, removed one cause completely and exposed two more. Three runs that change one thing each were submitted to tell those two apart, and two are in. Switching off the part of the wave model that grows waves from the local wind nearly doubles the wave reaching the beach, the opposite of what we predicted. And a deliberately wrong run that lifts the whole ocean edge of the model shows the bays follow the ocean one for one, so the missing water has to be added between the ocean and the bays, not at the edge.

Configuration

The reference setup

The “premier” is our reference configuration; every other run is compared against it, and each experiment changes exactly one thing relative to it.

Domain
Name and extentv3 — the whole Jersey shore from Cape May to Sandy Hook, plus Raritan Bay, Lower Bay and the Sandy Hook / Shrewsbury lobe; every back bay from Raritan Bay to Cape May Harbor is computed, not imposed. Frozen 26 August 2026.
Mesh3,412,470 cells on a nested grid at 200 / 100 / 50 / 25 m (25 m in the surf zone, on dunes, along bay margins and in the estuaries; 50 m over every bay and all low land).
Water-level boundaryThe 10 m depth contour along the open coast, plus short forced cross-sections at the Verrazzano Narrows and the mouth of the Arthur Kill, and a wedge across the Delaware Bay side of Cape May. 224 forcing points.
Elevation11 sources stacked best-first: USACE channel surveys (south, Raritan / Arthur Kill, NJ, Shrewsbury 2015), USACE 2010 topo-bathymetry, ConEd Raritan, NOAA CUDEM, the NJ 10-ft DEM, CUDEM 1/3 arc-second, GMRT. Terrain detail inside each cell is kept on an 8 × 8 sub-grid.
Forcing
Storm tideThe US Army Corps NACCS storm-tide hindcast of Sandy (an ADCIRC model coupled to the STWAVE wave model) at 224 points along the boundary, converted from 1992 mean sea level to NAVD88 with NOAA’s VDatum grids.
WavesNOAA’s CORA wave hindcast (the SWAN model on a fine coastal grid): wave height, period and direction at 36 points along the 10 m contour, fed to SnapWave.
Wind and pressureERA5 hourly 10 m wind and sea-level pressure (0.25°).
RainAORC hourly precipitation; infiltration effectively off.
RiversUSGS discharge at the gauged rivers (Raritan, Toms, Mullica, Great Egg, Tuckahoe and others).
Physics
HydrodynamicsSFINCS v2.3.3 (“Faber”): sub-grid continuity, momentum advection on, Coriolis on, viscosity 0.01, cells wet above 0.01 m, Manning roughness varying with land cover, weirs at the barrier islands’ known walls.
Waves (SnapWave)A steady-state wave solver recomputed every 30 min: breaking index 0.78, breaking coefficient 1, seabed friction 0.02, 5° direction bins over the full circle, growth by the local wind on, infragravity (long-period) waves off, up to 100 iterations. SnapWave is roughly 86 % of the run time.
Window00:00 28 Oct → 00:00 31 Oct 2012 (UTC), 1 h spin-up ramp; output every 10 min at gauges, hourly maps.
Validation set
High-water marks185 USGS marks inside the region; 94 scored after quality and depth screening (the median modelled water level within 50 m of each mark).
Gauges25 stations: NOAA (Sandy Hook, Atlantic City, Cape May, the Battery), USGS tidal and interior-bay gauges, and USGS storm-tide sensors.
Flood extentFEMA’s surge extent map (New Jersey only; 14.0 km² of New York land is left out of the score).
Scores

How the completed runs score

A high-water mark is a surveyed line left by the flood on a wall or a tree. We compare each one with the modelled water level within 50 m of it, using the same 94 marks for every run; RMSE is the typical size of the error and bias its average sign. The extent scores compare the modelled flood outline with FEMA’s map of how far the surge reached in New Jersey: CSI is the overall agreement (1 is perfect), POD the share of FEMA’s flooded area the model also floods, and FAR the share of the model’s flooded area that FEMA does not show. FEMA’s map does not cover New York, so 14 km² of New York land is left out of every extent score. A run with the wave model off is a legitimate setup, but its extent score is not on the same footing as one with waves, so it is flagged rather than ranked.

The rain-off row is not a candidate configuration, because Sandy’s rain really fell. It exists to measure how much of the model’s “false alarm” area is rain-fed wetting that FEMA’s surge-only map cannot contain, and the answer is 94 %. Its high-water-mark score collapses because eight marks that the rain filled go dry in that run; on the marks that stay wet it is 0.441 m.

The bottom row is the best-looking line in the table and is not a candidate either. It lifts the whole ocean by a quarter metre, which closes the gap in the southern bays by trading the oceanfront for the bays: the open-coast marks and the Atlantic City pier end up 20 to 30 cm too high. Compared mark by mark, it beats the no-waves run by 7 cm, with an uncertainty range that just touches zero, and is not distinguishable from the reference run. The wind-off wave run is being scored this morning and joins the table when it lands.

2 – 10 September

The week, in order

2–3 September — rain is nearly all of the false alarm

Switching the rain off raises the extent agreement from 0.71 to 0.81 and cuts the false-alarm share from 0.22 to 0.02. Measured directly, 93.7 % of the reference run’s “false alarm” area is wetting fed by rain, mostly marsh platforms and creeks joined to the surge, which a surge-only map cannot show. Two cautions came with it. Seven percent of FEMA’s flooded area is reached only when rain is on. And the marks around Lower Bay read 0.3 to 0.4 m higher with rain off, which cannot be a real effect of removing water: the bay sloshes back and forth on its own after any small disturbance, and the peak lands at a different point of that slosh. That puts a band of about ±0.3 m on any single run’s bay peak; our side-by-side comparisons are designed to allow for it.

3 September — the runs moved to scratch storage

Our home storage hit its 100 GB limit, and on this cluster that does not fail loudly: it cuts output files short while the job reports success. All the runs now live on the 1 TB scratch file system, a desktop copy was taken, and the scripts check the right quota before copying anything. Scratch is not backed up and deletes files untouched for 90 days, so the desktop copy is the one that lasts.

3–8 September — buildings in the flood model

Building footprints from the state and from Microsoft were obtained and added to the model’s terrain as blocks 4 m tall, so buildings take up space and narrow the paths water can flow through inside each grid cell. The first attempt had to be thrown away because of a quirk in the model-building software: putting the buildings layer first in the list of elevation sources made it re-grid the underlying terrain and shift 1.25 million cell heights, 29 of them by more than a metre. The rebuild paints the buildings onto the finished terrain instead. Scored properly, buildings make no measurable difference to Sandy outside the buildings themselves: the change in mark error is +0.8 cm, with an uncertainty range that includes zero. That is expected for a long, slow surge that fills in behind any obstacle; the buildings are now in place for faster storms where they will matter.

8 September — the low bias is a problem of waves not arriving

The question was why the open coast and the back bays run low. Three measurements answered it. First, what is missing is a steady amount of water, not a tide or a peak: at every southern bay gauge the model sits 0.2 to 0.55 m below the observations for the whole quiet day before the storm, while the tidal range is right to within a few percent and the ocean pier is matched to 6 mm. So shifting the whole model up by a constant would be the wrong fix; something that lifts the water behind the beaches is missing. Second, that something is wave setup: when big waves break on a beach they pile water against the shore, and during Sandy that pile should be 20 to 35 cm; the model makes about 5 cm. Third, the cause of the second: the waves enter the model along a seaward boundary line where we impose the wave conditions, and along the southern coast 43 % of the cells touching that line carried no waves at all. The line follows the 10 m depth contour, which on a square grid is a staircase, and every inner corner of a staircase is a cell the wave solver never updates. We confirmed that rule in the solver’s source code this week.

9 September — the redrawn boundary fixed the corners and exposed the shelf

The run with the redrawn boundary hit its 14-hour time limit at 55 % of the storm, because the wave grid grew from 1.8 to 2.9 million cells; it was resubmitted with a 40-hour limit and finishes tomorrow. What it had written by then, up to 16:00 on 29 October, was enough to test the criterion we had set in advance: do the waves get through, rather than do the scores improve.

  • The dead corners are gone. None of the 2,381 cells next to the new boundary is dead, against 2,580 of 6,556 on the reference run at the same hour.
  • The boundary passes waves in, unevenly. The long eastern leg and the south-facing steps hand 70 to 85 % of the imposed wave height to the first cell inside. The bottom edge south of Cape May hands over only about a third along its shallow western half, and we have ruled out cell size, wave breaking and wave direction as the reason; it is not yet explained.
  • The wave then loses half its height crossing the shelf. Within 10 km of the line it falls to about half the imposed value and stays there. NOAA’s wave model keeps 60 to 80 % across the same water. The solver’s source code shows that its only way of losing wave energy on the open shelf is friction against the seabed, and at the friction setting we use, a 6 m swell with a 13.6 s period in 18 m of water loses 23 % of its height every 10 km, which is most of what we measured. Halving that coefficient to the software’s default halves the loss.
  • Sandy’s waves came from the south. Through the rise and peak of the storm the waves arrive from between south-southeast and south, so they travel north, parallel to the 200 km eastern leg of the boundary, and the short bottom edge and the steps are where the energy actually has to enter. That geometry is why the previous point matters so much.
  • A quarter of the wave calculations do not settle, and those hours are unphysical. The wave model recomputes a steady wave field every 30 minutes by repeating its calculation until the answer stops changing. In 25 of the first 80 of those it never stopped changing; in those hours wave heights of up to 22 m appear across tens of thousands of shelf cells, and a persistent hot spot east of Sandy Hook sits on cells the flood model uses. Our main suspect is the term that grows waves from the local wind, which now acts over 1.1 million cells of open shelf where before it had only a few cells to work on.

In one sentence: the geometric fix worked, and it showed that the wave model is losing the imposed wave energy to seabed friction, and in the hours before the storm to numerical noise, before the waves reach the beach where their setup would lift the beaches and the bays.

10 September — wind off doubles the wave at the beach; lifting the ocean lifts everything

Two of the three new runs finished overnight. The two long runs, the redrawn-boundary rerun 21 hours in and the lower-friction run 19 hours in, were pushed off their computers by the cluster’s scheduler at 08:30 in the same second and started again from zero, so they now finish around midday on the 11th. What they had written was saved before the restarts overwrote it, and read.

  • Wind off is the big lever, and we predicted the opposite. With the wind-growth term switched off, the run took under 6 hours instead of 28; 8 of the 145 wave calculations failed to settle instead of 25 of 80; the runaway 22 m waves and the hot spot east of Sandy Hook are gone; and the wave reaching the inner shelf nearly doubled (chart below). We had written down that this switch would not move it much. Our reading: the wind term only ever adds wave energy, with nothing to take it away, and over a million cells it stopped the solver from settling; the unsettled answers were too low on the shelf, not just spiky. The cost is that waves inside the bays drop to nearly zero, because in this model the wind term was the only thing making them, and Sandy did raise half-metre chop in Barnegat Bay.
  • Friction is a distant second. From its saved partial run, halving the seabed friction moved the same number by 0.02 to 0.12, short of the 0.6 we had set. By its own test, friction is not what was holding the waves back.
  • Lifting the ocean edge lifted everything by the same quarter metre. Raising the ocean boundary by the beach-setup formula raised the pre-storm level at every southern bay gauge by 22 to 31 cm, closing most of the bay gap, and raised the Atlantic City pier by 33 cm, where it is now 32 cm too high (chart below). The bays follow the boundary one for one, and so does the open ocean. What the observations show is the bays sitting above the pier, and no uniform lift can create that difference: whatever is missing acts between the pier and the bay, through the surf zone and the inlets.
  • Restart files are now in place. Every run set up from today saves its state every 6 hours; a run that gets pushed off its computer now resumes from the last save and the pieces are joined back into one output. Checked on a small test model: the resumed run matches an uninterrupted one to within the solver’s own run-to-run noise.

In one sentence: the wave model was not short of wave energy, it was failing to settle on an answer; and the water missing from the bays has to be added between the ocean and the bays, not at the ocean edge.

Running now

Four runs, one change each: two finished, two restarted

Each run is judged first on whether the waves get through, using the predictions below, which were written before any result was read, and only then on scores. Status as of the morning of 10 September.

Why the third run is wrong on purpose. The published rule (Leijnse et al. 2025) is that a formula for wave setup at the boundary and a wave model are never used together, and the storm-tide hindcast we use already includes the setup that builds up seaward of the 10 m contour. Adding beach setup at that boundary lifts the whole shelf, which is wrong at the ocean gauge by construction. We run it only to learn the most that a correct wave setup could ever close of the gap. The run-up half of the same formula, the swash, is deliberately left out: it is an up-and-down motion, not a level, so it cannot lift a bay or a gauge average; its effect on open-beach marks is assessed separately without a run.

Decisions ahead

What we are not doing, and what comes next

  • Still not switching wave models. The 70 % line we had set as the trigger is now cleared at two of the four sites with the wind term off alone, and the failure turned out to be the solver not settling, not a missing piece of physics. The tool stays.
  • Next run (recommended, your call): wind off plus friction 0.01, one 6-hour run. The two changes are independent and both moved the number the right way. If they add up, Atlantic City and Sea Bright clear the 0.85 target and only the Cape May stretch is left.
  • Reopening the shallower boundary for the Cape May stretch. On the 9th we ruled out moving the line closer to shore because friction over a wide shallow band looked bad. That reasoning assumed friction was the problem, and it was not. The western half of the bottom edge passes a third of the imposed wave even with the wind term off, and imposing NOAA’s waves nearer to where they are needed is the fix for that edge.
  • Bay chop. Switching the wind term off removes the half-metre waves Sandy raised inside Barnegat Bay. What we score is water level, and bay waves add only a few centimetres at bay shores; we will put a number on what was lost before worrying about it.
  • Coarsening the shelf band is still the right platform, but less urgent: the wind change already cut a wave run from 28 hours to 6.
  • Tell the model’s developers about the calculations that fail to settle, with the hours and the grid size. A wind term with nothing to balance it is a known limitation, and there may be a setting for it that is not exposed.
  • Tomorrow: the two restarted runs land around midday; full read-out, side-by-side scores against the reference run, and the wind-off run’s scores added to the table above.
Every number here is recorded with its conditions in the project’s working notes; high-water-mark statistics use the median modelled level within 50 m of each mark unless stated.
